To ingratiate yourself means to deliberately make someone like you or approve of you — usually through flattery, excessive helpfulness, charm, or pleasing behavior — often because you want to gain something from them, like power, money, a promotion, or social acceptance.

The key idea is that the behavior is calculated and self-serving, not genuinely kind. The person doing it has a hidden motive: get this person on my side so I can benefit.
How It Is Almost Always Used

This verb almost always appears in one specific pattern:

ingratiate + [reflexive pronoun] + with + [person]

The reflexive pronoun (myself, yourself, himself, herself, themselves) is almost always required. You don't ingratiate someone else — you ingratiate yourself with someone. Think of it as directing the action back at yourself: you are the one making yourself more likable in someone else's eyes.

Examples:

  • She tried to ingratiate herself with her new boss by volunteering for every task.
  • He ingratiated himself with the wealthy family by constantly praising their home and lifestyle.
  • The new student ingratiated himself with the popular group by always agreeing with whatever they said.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

This is crucial: ingratiate almost always carries a negative or suspicious tone. When you use this word to describe someone's behavior, you are usually implying that:

  • Their niceness is fake or exaggerated
  • They are not being genuine — they are performing kindness
  • They have an ulterior motive — they want something
  • Their behavior is a little shameless or undignified

If someone is simply being kind, you would not use this word. You use "ingratiate" when the kindness feels strategic, excessive, or hollow.

A good employee who works hard to impress their boss → not ingratiation.
An employee who showers the boss with compliments, laughs at every joke, and brings them coffee every morning specifically to get a promotion → ingratiation.

The difference is sincerity. Ingratiation is niceness used as a tool.

Ingratiation is what people informally describe as:

  • "sucking up"
  • "buttering someone up"
  • "brown-nosing"
  • "currying favor"

These phrases all describe the same act: performing charm or helpfulness to win someone's approval for personal gain. "Ingratiate" is simply the formal, more sophisticated way to say the same thing.

• Ingratiating (adjective) — describes behavior or manner that is designed to win favor. "He had an ingratiating smile — the kind that made you feel like he wanted something." It can also be used neutrally or even positively to mean "charming," but the suspicious undertone is usually still present.
  • Ingratiatingly (adverb) — in a manner meant to win favor. "She spoke ingratiatingly, agreeing with everything the director said."
  • Ingratiation (noun) — the act itself. "His ingratiation with the committee was obvious to everyone."

Ingratiation is different from simply being likable. A naturally warm and friendly person is not ingratiating — they are just pleasant. Ingratiation implies conscious strategy. The person has made a decision: "I will behave in this specific way to make this specific person like me so I can get what I want."

This is why the word tends to sound slightly contemptuous. It strips the "niceness" of its moral value, because the niceness isn't really about the other person at all — it's about the self.
One Final Example to Tie It All Together

After the new manager arrived, David suddenly started arriving early, complimenting her decisions in every meeting, and offering to handle her administrative tasks. Everyone in the office could see he was simply trying to ingratiate himself with her before the annual performance reviews.

Notice what this sentence tells you: David's behavior changed because of a motive. It wasn't who he naturally was. He was performing — and doing it transparently enough that his coworkers saw right through it. That is the essence of the word.
